segments.name: The House of the Italian Exile

stops.name: 38 Charlotte Street, Portland Place, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from christina_rossetti.journey.json, which pins the same Hallam Street room; the corrected street position of 110 Hallam Street is 51.5202, -0.1454, about 190 m south, and the discrepancy is recorded in the report rather than silently fixed.
stops.campa: At 38 Charlotte Street off Portland Place a second son is born to Gabriele Rossetti, the Neapolitan poet who fled Naples under a death sentence for the constitutional rising, and to Frances Polidori, whose brother was Byron's physician. They name him Gabriel Charles Dante. The rooms fill with exiles arguing the Commedia over tea, the father certain that Dante hid an anti-papal cipher in it. Two years later Christina Rossetti is born in the same room. The street is renumbered Hallam Street before the century ends, and a plaque goes up on the wall.
suggested_refs: The English Heritage blue plaque at 110 Hallam Street, formerly 38 Charlotte Street, Portland Place

stops.name: King's College School, the Strand
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the school; the year is contradicted between sources. The Victorian Web chronology gives entry in 1837, the geography material used for this file gives 1836. Not resolved. Month set to September by school convention, not by document.
stops.campa: He is entered in the junior department of King's College School, in the basement rooms under the college on the Strand, where his father teaches Italian to paying pupils by the hour. The boy takes French, Latin, and the whole run of English poetry, and leaves at thirteen with no intention of a university. The family has moved across the road to 50 Charlotte Street and will stay there fifteen years. Gabriele's students come and go through the same door his son crosses each morning; the household economy is lessons sold one at a time.
suggested_refs: The Strand buildings of King's College, whose basement housed the school in the 1830s
sources: Victorian Web, 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti: An Annotated Chronology'

stops.name: Sass's Drawing Academy, Bloomsbury
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of entry; month unknown and defaulted. The street address of the academy is not confirmed in any source reached, so the pin is a Bloomsbury approximation and is stated as such in the report.
stops.campa: At Henry Sass's drawing academy in Bloomsbury he does the ordinary preparatory work of a boy aiming at the Royal Academy: charcoal, the antique, the human figure broken into its parts and drawn again. The exact house is not recorded in any source reached. In the same years he is translating Burger's Lenore and pieces of the Nibelungenlied out of German for his own amusement, and beginning the Italian versions that will become The Early Italian Poets. He is fourteen.
suggested_refs: Henry Sass's academy, the standard preparatory route into the Royal Academy Schools

stops.name: Royal Academy Antique School, Trafalgar Square
stops.date_confidence: attested with a sequence dispute. The Rossetti Archive gives 1846 for admission to the Antique School, after probationer status in 1844 and full studentship in December 1845; Wikipedia gives 1845 for the Antique School. The commonly repeated order, probationer in 1846 and student afterwards, is inverted and is not followed here.
stops.campa: Admitted at last to the Antique School of the Royal Academy, then housed in the east wing of the National Gallery building on Trafalgar Square, he draws from plaster casts and grows impatient inside a year. He signs himself Dante Gabriel now, moving his namesake to the front: Dante Alighieri, whose Vita Nuova he is already Englishing line by line, and whose Beatrice he will paint for forty years under four different faces. Within two years he is writing to a painter outside the Academy, asking to be taken as a pupil instead.
suggested_refs: The Royal Academy Schools in the east wing of the National Gallery, Trafalgar Square
Rossetti's manuscript translations of the Vita Nuova

stops.name: Ford Madox Brown's studio, Fitzrovia
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1848 by the standard biography; day unknown and defaulted. Studio coordinates are a Fitzrovia approximation, the address not being recovered.
stops.campa: He writes to Ford Madox Brown, a painter seven years his senior whose work he has seen and admired, asking to be taken as a pupil. Brown, amused rather than flattered, accepts and sets him to painting pickle jars from life. Rossetti lasts a matter of weeks at the jars and the formal arrangement lapses, but the friendship holds thirty-four years, to the day Brown designs the stone over his grave. The pickle jars are the only formal instruction he takes outside the Academy. He finishes no course of study anywhere.
suggested_refs: Rossetti's letter of March 1848 asking Ford Madox Brown to take him as a pupil
sources: Oswald Doughty, 'A Victorian Romantic', as quoted in reachable secondary sources

stops.name: Cleveland Street, the studio shared with Hunt
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1848; month unknown and defaulted to the summer before the Brotherhood is named. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from william_holman_hunt.journey.json.
stops.campa: He seeks out William Holman Hunt after seeing The Eve of St Agnes at the Academy exhibition and finds a painter his own age already doing what he has only argued for. They take rooms together on Cleveland Street, and Rossetti begins The Girlhood of Mary Virgin there, with Christina Rossetti sitting for the Virgin and their mother for St Anne. Hunt works from the thing itself, hour by hour, in hard light. Rossetti works from what he has read. Neither converts the other, and the two methods hold the Brotherhood together for three years.
suggested_refs: Hunt's 'The Eve of St Agnes', the picture that brought Rossetti to his door

stops.name: 83 Gower Street, the seven names
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1848; the exact day is not recorded in the reachable sources and is defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from john_everett_millais.journey.json and william_holman_hunt.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the Millais family house on Gower Street seven young men give themselves a name. Rossetti, Hunt, and John Everett Millais agree on truth to nature against the sloshy manner they trace to Raphael; James Collinson, Thomas Woolner, Frederic George Stephens, and William Michael Rossetti as secretary make up the seven. The name looks back deliberately at Johann Friedrich Overbeck's Lukasbund, founded in Vienna in 1809 by young men who also walked out of an academy to paint like the century before Raphael. They agree to sign nothing but the initials.
suggested_refs: The Millais family house at 83 Gower Street, Bloomsbury
The Lukasbund of 1809, acknowledged model for the Brotherhood's name

stops.name: Free Exhibition, Hyde Park Corner, the two letters
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1849 by the Rossetti Archive chronology; day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The Girlhood of Mary Virgin hangs at the Free Exhibition in the Chinese Gallery at Hyde Park Corner, the first picture shown in public with the letters P.R.B. beside the signature, and nobody yet knows what they stand for. Rossetti has exhibited ahead of Hunt and Millais, outside the Academy, on purpose. Within a year the four issues of The Germ carry the finished text of The Blessed Damozel and seven poems by his sister, and the press has worked out what the initials mean and begun to swing.
stops.quote: The blessed damozel lean'd out / From the gold bar of Heaven; / Her eyes were deeper than the depth / Of waters still'd at even; / She had three lilies in her hand, / And the stars in her hair were seven.
stops.quote_source: 'The Blessed Damozel', opening stanza, first printed in The Germ, 1850; text from Representative Poetry Online, University of Toronto
suggested_refs: 'The Girlhood of Mary Virgin' (Tate), the first picture signed P.R.B.
The four issues of The Germ, January to April 1850

stops.name: Musee du Louvre, the Old Masters with Hunt
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1849 as the first leg of the Paris and Belgium trip; the day is approximate within the month.
stops.campa: He crosses to Paris with Hunt in September and spends the days in the Louvre, working through the Old Masters with a notebook and a running argument. The Academy reveres the high Renaissance. He walks through it to the rooms before it: the early Italians, the gold grounds, the flat certainty of pictures painted for altars rather than for collectors. He writes sonnets on the pictures as he goes and sends them home in letters. The trip is a study tour with almost no drawing to show for it.
suggested_refs: Rossetti's sonnets written on pictures seen in the Louvre, autumn 1849
sources: Victorian Web, 'D.G. Rossetti's Trip to Paris and Belgium'

stops.name: Musees Royaux des Beaux-Arts, Brussels
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1849; day unknown and defaulted. Coordinates corrected before use: the figure in circulation carried a London latitude and landed in the Netherlands some 75 km north of the city.
stops.campa: At the royal collections in Brussels the two Englishmen look at Flemish painting they cannot see at home, which is the point of the whole circuit. Hunt takes notes on method, on grounds and glazes and the drying of whites. Rossetti takes notes on subject. Between Brussels, Antwerp and Ghent they see more fifteenth-century painting in three weeks than either has seen in a lifetime of the National Gallery, and the Brotherhood's programme, until now an argument in a room on Gower Street, acquires a set of actual pictures behind it.
suggested_refs: The Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Rue de la Regence, Brussels
sources: Victorian Web, 'D.G. Rossetti's Trip to Paris and Belgium'

stops.name: St Bavo's Cathedral, Ghent, the Van Eyck altarpiece
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1849; the day is approximate, placed before the Bruges letter of 25 October.
stops.campa: In St Bavo's they stand before the Ghent Altarpiece, the Van Eyck brothers' panels in the chapel they were painted for. Here is everything the Brotherhood has been claiming in the abstract: every leaf and jewel and hair rendered without hierarchy, the whole surface equally awake, and no trace of the grand manner the Academy teaches as the only manner. Rossetti is twenty-one. He will never paint like this and never stop citing it. The sacristan shows the wings for a fee, one at a time, and the two of them pay.
suggested_refs: The Ghent Altarpiece of Hubert and Jan van Eyck, St Bavo's Cathedral
sources: Victorian Web, 'D.G. Rossetti's Trip to Paris and Belgium'

stops.name: St John's Hospital, Bruges, the Memling panels
stops.date_confidence: attested by Rossetti's own letter of 25 October 1849.
stops.campa: From Bruges on the twenty-fifth of October he writes home that the miraculous works of Memling and Van Eyck are by far the best of all he has seen, and the judgment does not soften with age. In the old hospital of St John the Memling panels hang in the room they were made for, small and still and lit from one window. He writes a sonnet on Memling for The Germ before the year is out. The Flemish circuit ends here, and the two of them turn back for London and for the reviews.
suggested_refs: Memling's panels in the Sint-Janshospitaal, Bruges
Rossetti's letter of 25 October 1849
sources: Rossetti letter of 25 October 1849, quoted at rossettiarchive.org and Victorian Web

stops.name: Cranbourne Alley, the milliner's back room
stops.date_confidence: contested year. The sources reached give the Deverell encounter as 1849 or as 1850; month and day are nowhere recorded and are defaulted. Not resolved.
stops.campa: Walter Deverell, shopping with his mother in Cranbourne Alley near Leicester Square, sees a tall red-haired assistant in a back room of the milliner's and asks her to sit. Elizabeth Siddal poses first as Viola for Deverell's Twelfth Night, then for the circle at large, then, within two years, for Rossetti and almost no one else. He draws her hundreds of times: reading, sewing, sleeping, at a window, her head fallen sideways. He teaches her to paint, and he stops letting the others use her.
suggested_refs: Deverell's 'Twelfth Night', Elizabeth Siddal's first sitting
Rossetti's drawings of Siddal, Ashmolean Museum
sources: COVE chronology, 'Siddal discovered by Walter Deverell'
Merryn Allingham, 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Elizabeth Siddal'

stops.name: 17 Red Lion Square, the first rooms of his own
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1851 by the Survey of London and by the plaque text; month and day unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: He takes lodgings and a working room at 17 Red Lion Square, his first address away from his parents. Five years after he leaves, the same rooms are taken by William Morris and Edward Burne-Jones, who cannot buy furniture they are willing to look at and so design their own, huge and painted and built by a local carpenter. Rossetti visits and writes about it to Scotland. The second Pre-Raphaelite generation begins in a room he has vacated. The plaque put up in 1911 names all three of them.
stops.quote: intensely mediaeval furniture ... tables and chairs like incubi and succubi
stops.quote_source: Rossetti on Morris's Red Lion Square furniture, quoted in J. W. Mackail, 'The Life of William Morris', ch. 4 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The 1911 London County Council plaque at 17 Red Lion Square naming Rossetti, Morris and Burne-Jones
sources: Survey of London via British History Online
J. W. Mackail, 'The Life of William Morris', ch. 4

stops.name: 14 Chatham Place, Blackfriars Bridge
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1852 for the move; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The status and date of the engagement to Siddal are reported inconsistently across sources and are left unresolved.
stops.campa: He moves to rooms over the river at 14 Chatham Place by Blackfriars Bridge and keeps them ten years. Siddal is installed there, and the two are understood to be engaged. Pictures are not selling. He looks into a post as a telegraph operator with the Great Northern Railway and then, instead, turns to small watercolours a man can finish in a week and a buyer can afford. The Thames goes past the window brown and busy; he paints Dante and Beatrice above it.
suggested_refs: The vanished Chatham Place frontage by Blackfriars Bridge, redeveloped in the 1860s

stops.name: Working Men's College, Red Lion Square, teaching beside Ruskin
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1854 for both the Ruskin introduction and the teaching; month and day defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from john_ruskin.journey.json and william_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: Robert McCracken of Belfast buys an ink drawing of Dante and brings Rossetti to the notice of John Ruskin, who becomes his patron and buys steadily for years. Ruskin teaches drawing without pay at F. D. Maurice's Working Men's College in Red Lion Square, and Rossetti teaches beside him, with Ford Madox Brown, in a room of clerks and joiners learning to look. A young Oxford man named Edward Burne-Jones comes to watch the class and never leaves the circle again.
stops.quote: When I left Oxford I got to know Rossetti, whose friendship I sought and obtained... He taught me practically all I ever learnt; afterwards I made a method for myself to suit my nature.
suggested_refs: The Working Men's College founded by F. D. Maurice, 1854, Red Lion Square

segments.name: Oxford: the Union and Jane Burden

stops.name: Exeter College, Oxford, the two undergraduates
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1856 for the first contact; month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The college pin is approximate to Morris and Burne-Jones's Exeter rooms, the meetings themselves falling partly in London.
stops.campa: Two undergraduates at Exeter College, William Morris and Edward Burne-Jones, are running a magazine and have decided between them that Rossetti is the greatest man alive. He meets them, recruits them for the Oxford and Cambridge Magazine, and tells them both to give up whatever they were going to do and paint. Morris has money, a temper, and no training. Burne-Jones has no money and no training either. Rossetti has never taught anyone successfully and does not begin now, and both of them obey.
stops.quote: Two young men, projectors of the Oxford and Cambridge Magazine, have recently come to town from Oxford and are now very intimate friends of mine. Their names are Morris and Jones. They have turned artists instead of taking up any other career to which the University generally leads, and both are men of real genius.
stops.quote_source: Rossetti to William Bell Scott, February 1857, quoted in J. W. Mackail, 'The Life of William Morris', ch. 4 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The Oxford and Cambridge Magazine, 1856, twelve monthly numbers
sources: J. W. Mackail, 'The Life of William Morris', ch. 4

stops.name: Oxford Union, the Arthurian bays
stops.date_confidence: attested: work ran August to November 1857 and was broken off in mid-November. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json; the Union's Old Library is in fact at about 51.7529, -1.2593, some 400 m south-west, and the inherited pin is kept for atlas continuity with the discrepancy recorded in the report.
stops.campa: Benjamin Woodward's new debating hall has a gallery of blank bays under the roof, and Rossetti offers to fill them for nothing but expenses. He assembles a team of amateurs: Morris, Burne-Jones, Arthur Hughes, Val Prinsep, Spencer-Stanhope, Pollen. They paint Malory subjects in distemper straight onto unprepared brick, on scaffolds, through a summer of practical jokes and soda water. His own bay is Sir Lancelot's Vision of the Sanc Grael. Within months the colours begin sinking into the wall, and the work stops in November when Siddal falls ill at Matlock.
stops.quote: the stillest creature that ever breathed out of an oyster shell
stops.quote_source: Rossetti on the architect Benjamin Woodward, quoted in J. W. Mackail, 'The Life of William Morris', ch. 4 (Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The Oxford Union murals in the Old Debating Hall, now the Library

stops.name: Oxford, the theatre and Jane Burden
stops.date_confidence: contested. The Rossetti Archive dates the encounter to September 1857 and names Rossetti and Morris; the Ashmolean and the Burne-Jones biography name Rossetti and Burne-Jones. Date and coordinates inherited byte-identical from jane_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json, which carry October 1857 and the Burne-Jones version. Not resolved.
stops.campa: At a performance by the touring Drury Lane company they notice a girl in the audience, seventeen, a stableman's daughter from Holywell Street with a face nobody in the room has a category for. Jane Burden agrees to sit. Her sister Elizabeth is with her and goes unrecorded. Rossetti draws her in pencil that autumn and will use the same head for twenty-five years, as Beatrice, as Proserpine, as Astarte. Morris, who cannot draw her, writes on the back of his failed attempt that he cannot paint her but loves her, and marries her in 1859.
stops.quote: MISS JANE BURDEN (Mrs. William Morris), aet. 17. From the original pencil drawing by D. G. Rossetti
stops.quote_source: Caption to Rossetti's 1857 pencil drawing of Jane Burden, inherited from jane_morris.journey.json
suggested_refs: Rossetti's pencil drawing of Jane Burden at seventeen, 1857

segments.name: Marriage, the Firm, and the Grave at Highgate

stops.name: 14 Chatham Place, Bocca Baciata
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1859 for the painting; month and day unrecorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: At Chatham Place he paints Fanny Cornforth's head and shoulders close up against the picture plane, filling the panel with hair, a marigold, an apple, and a mouth, and calls it Bocca Baciata after Boccaccio's line about the kissed mouth that renews itself like the moon. The medieval crowds and the small watercolours stop here. What follows for twenty years is one woman, half-length, in front of flowers, painted large and sold to northern manufacturers. Hunt, seeing it, thinks the Brotherhood's programme has been abandoned for something gross.
suggested_refs: 'Bocca Baciata' (1859), Museum of Fine Arts, Boston

stops.name: St Clement's, Hastings Old Town, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Hastings parish record and local press.
stops.campa: After nearly ten years of an engagement broken and resumed, and with Siddal too weak to walk, they marry at St Clement's in the Old Town with no family present on either side. She is carried the short distance to the church. He has written to his mother the week before that if he does not marry her now he will lose her, and nobody from Charlotte Street comes. They go on to Paris and Boulogne for the summer. A sanctuary lamp in the church commemorates the marriage long after both of them are dead.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary lamp at St Clement's, Hastings, commemorating the Rossetti marriage
sources: St Clement's, Hastings Old Town parish history
Merryn Allingham, 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Elizabeth Siddal'

stops.name: Red House, Bexleyheath, painting the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1860 and 1861 for the decoration; month defaulted. Coordinates corrected before use: the figure in circulation lay about 1.3 km east of the house.
stops.campa: Philip Webb has built Morris a red brick house in the Kent orchards, and the circle descends on it to decorate every surface: painted furniture, embroidered hangings, wall paintings out of Malory and the Nibelungenlied. Rossetti comes with Siddal, Burne-Jones with Georgiana, Ford Madox Brown with his brushes. Nothing is bought that can be made. Out of these weekends comes the decision to sell the work rather than keep it, and within a year the firm exists. Morris holds the house five years and is then forced to sell it.
suggested_refs: Red House, Bexleyheath, built by Philip Webb 1859-1860, now National Trust

stops.name: 8 Red Lion Square, the Firm founded
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 April 1861. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json and edward_burne_jones.journey.json.
stops.campa: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co., Fine Art Workmen in Painting, Carving, Furniture and the Metals, is founded at 8 Red Lion Square with seven partners: Morris, Rossetti, Burne-Jones, Ford Madox Brown, Philip Webb, Peter Paul Marshall, Charles Faulkner. Rossetti designs stained glass and painted panels and draws against the work. Hunt, who was there on Gower Street thirteen years before, is not asked. The firm will outlast the Brotherhood by half a century, and Rossetti will be bought out of it.
suggested_refs: The 1861 prospectus of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co.

stops.name: 14 Chatham Place, the laudanum
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1862; the day of the overdose is given as 10 or 11 February in different accounts and the inquest verdict was accidental death.
stops.campa: Elizabeth Siddal Rossetti dies of laudanum in the rooms over the river, not long after a stillborn daughter. He has come home late from the Working Men's College and found her; the bottle is empty, and a note, by one account, is destroyed before the inquest. The verdict is accidental death. He is thirty-three and has been married twenty-one months. The Thames is at the window as it always was. He does not paint in the rooms again, does not sleep in them again, and leaves Chatham Place inside the year.
stops.quote: The woodspurge has a cup of three.
stops.quote_source: 'The Woodspurge', written 1856, published 1870; text from Wikiquote, Dante Gabriel Rossetti
suggested_refs: The 1862 inquest into the death of Elizabeth Siddal Rossetti

stops.name: Highgate Cemetery West, the book in the coffin
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1862; the burial day is approximate within the week following the death. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from christina_rossetti.journey.json.
stops.campa: At the burial in the family plot at Highgate he puts the only manuscript of his recent poems into the coffin, wound in her hair against her cheek, and Ford Madox Brown is one of the few who watch him do it. Several of the poems exist nowhere else. His father Gabriele lies in the same ground, eight years dead. The gesture is understood by everyone present as final, and it is reported as final for seven years, until the man who arranges the reversal turns out to be on his payroll.
suggested_refs: The Rossetti family plot, Highgate Cemetery West, Swains Lane

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, taking the lease
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 October 1862 by the Rossetti Archive; the chronology in circulation says November, which is wrong. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from christina_rossetti.journey.json and jane_morris.journey.json; the house itself stands at about 51.4839, -0.1658, some 480 m east, and the discrepancy is recorded in the report.
stops.campa: He takes Tudor House on Cheyne Walk, a river frontage in Chelsea with a walled garden and more rooms than one man needs, and fills them with sub-tenants: Algernon Swinburne, George Meredith, his brother William Michael. Meredith lasts months. Swinburne stays two years and is not restful. Rossetti buys blue and white china, old mirrors, Japanese screens and heavy oak, and begins the collection that will make the house famous and the dealers rich. He lives here for the last twenty years of his life.
suggested_refs: Tudor House, also called the Queen's House, 16 Cheyne Walk, Chelsea, Historic England listed

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, the camera in the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested to 7 June 1865. Date and coordinates inherited byte-identical from jane_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: He hires the photographer John Robert Parsons for a day and spends it arranging Jane Morris in the garden and the front rooms: the loose dress without stays, the hair undone, the hands placed, the head tilted back over the canvas of the garden tent. Parsons works the camera; Rossetti works the pose. The negatives become his reference for a decade of paintings made when she is not in the room. He pays Parsons by the day and keeps the negatives, which end up in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
suggested_refs: The Parsons photographs of Jane Morris, 7 June 1865, Victoria and Albert Museum

stops.name: Penkill Castle, Ayrshire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1869; month and day approximate.
stops.campa: William Bell Scott takes him north to Penkill in Ayrshire, where Alice Boyd keeps the castle and Scott is painting the King's Quair up the stairwell. Rossetti walks the glen, reads his old poems aloud from memory, and finds he cannot recall whole stanzas of what he buried. Scott and Boyd hear him say so more than once. Christina Rossetti has been a guest in these rooms too, in other summers. He goes home in the autumn having decided something he does not put in writing.
suggested_refs: William Bell Scott's King's Quair mural in the stairwell at Penkill Castle

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, the wombat and the peacock clause
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1869 for the acquisition of the wombat Top; day unrecorded and defaulted. The often-repeated claim that peacocks were banned in all future Cadogan leases is legendary embellishment on a real clause and is treated as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The garden at Cheyne Walk fills with animals: wallabies, a raccoon, armadillos that dig under the neighbours' fences, a zebu bought because its eyes recalled Jane Morris, peacocks whose noise makes Lord Cadogan write a ban on peacocks into the ground lease. In September he acquires a wombat, names it Top after Morris, lets it sleep in the epergne at dinner, and draws himself weeping over it in ink when it dies inside the year. Whistler and Swinburne come to look. The house becomes a thing people describe in letters.
suggested_refs: Rossetti's pen drawing of himself mourning his wombat, 1869
The Public Domain Review essay 'O Uommibatto'

stops.name: Highgate Cemetery West, the grave opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to the night of 5 October 1869, with a Home Secretary's licence and legal witnesses.
stops.campa: On the night of the fifth of October, seven and a half years after the burial, the grave at Highgate is opened by lantern under a Home Secretary's licence, with a solicitor and a doctor standing by as witnesses. Charles Augustus Howell, his agent, has arranged it and is there; Rossetti is not. The notebook comes up wormholed and stinking and is disinfected leaf by leaf. Every page of the poem Jenny has a hole through it. He writes to his brother ten days later in a tone that is almost businesslike.
stops.quote_source: Rossetti to William Michael Rossetti, 15 October 1869, cited by the English Faculty, University of Cambridge
suggested_refs: The exhumed manuscript notebook of 1862, recovered 5 October 1869
sources: English Faculty, University of Cambridge, on the Rossetti exhumation

stops.name: Scalands Gate, Sussex, resting his eyes
stops.date_confidence: attested by Rossetti's letter to Burne-Jones of 13 March 1870 written from the house; earlier visits are recorded without dates.
stops.campa: His eyes have been failing and the doctors order him out of London, so he goes to Barbara Bodichon's house in the Sussex weald and writes to Burne-Jones from there in March that he can see well enough to be frightened. Jane Morris is at Hastings a few miles off, taking the sea air for her own health, and they are in the same country for the first time with Morris in neither place. Bodichon had once hoped this air might do something for Siddal's lungs. The proofs of the new book follow him down.
suggested_refs: Barbara Bodichon's Scalands Gate, near Robertsbridge, Sussex
sources: Burne-Jones Catalogue Raisonne, letter of 13 March 1870
Great British Life, Barbara Bodichon profile

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, Poems by D. G. Rossetti
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1870 for publication; the day is approximate within the month.
stops.campa: Poems by D. G. Rossetti appears in April and runs through five editions inside the year, carrying the first installment of The House of Life along with the pieces cut out of the ground at Highgate. He is forty-one and has published no book of his own verse before this one. The reviews are warm, and the warmest are written by men he knows and has asked: Swinburne in the Fortnightly, William Michael elsewhere. The one review he has not arranged is being drafted that summer under a false name.
stops.quote: A Sonnet is a moment's monument,-- / Memorial from the Soul's eternity / To one dead deathless hour.
stops.quote_source: 'The House of Life', introductory sonnet; text from Wikiquote, Dante Gabriel Rossetti
suggested_refs: 'Poems by D. G. Rossetti', F. S. Ellis, London, 1870

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the joint lease
stops.date_confidence: attested: Morris and Rossetti agreed the lease on 20 May 1871 and took occupation that summer. The date of 1869 sometimes given for the lease is wrong. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json and jane_morris.journey.json; the manor stands at about 51.6883, -1.6381.
stops.campa: Morris finds an Elizabethan farmhouse in a bend of the upper Thames and takes the lease jointly with Rossetti from the farmer Charles Hobbs, an arrangement neither of them explains to anyone. Weeks later Morris sails for Iceland. Rossetti stays at Kelmscott through the summer with Jane Morris and the two daughters, Jenny and May Morris, painting Jane in the meadow with the willows behind her. The village calls him the gentleman at the manor. The whole thing is conducted with the doors open and nothing said.
suggested_refs: Kelmscott Manor, Oxfordshire
Rossetti's 'Water Willow' (1871), Delaware Art Museum, painted at Kelmscott

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, the fleshly school
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1871 for the Contemporary Review article and May 1872 for the expanded pamphlet; the two are frequently conflated and are kept apart here. Day of the issue defaulted.
stops.campa: In the Contemporary Review a critic signing himself Thomas Maitland devotes an article to the fleshly school of poetry and to Rossetti as its chief practitioner: sensual, affected, morbid, indecent. Rossetti answers in the Athenaeum under his own name, and the pseudonym collapses into Robert Buchanan, a poet with grievances of his own. In May the article becomes a pamphlet at twice the length. Rossetti, on chloral to sleep and reading his post at Cheyne Walk, begins to believe the attack is organised and that strangers in the street are in on it.
suggested_refs: Robert Buchanan, 'The Fleshly School of Poetry and Other Phenomena of the Day', 1872

stops.name: Roehampton, the bottle of laudanum
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 June 1872 at the house of Dr Thomas Gordon Hake at Roehampton. The account placing the overdose at 16 Cheyne Walk is wrong. No street address for Hake's house was recovered, so the pin is a district approximation.
stops.campa: Removed to the house of Dr Thomas Gordon Hake at Roehampton to be watched, he is left alone for the night and takes a bottle of laudanum he has carried there in his coat. It is the drug that killed his wife, and roughly the same quantity. He is not found until the following afternoon and does not wake for a day and a half after that. Hake, a physician as well as a friend, has the sense to keep it out of the papers. Ten years and four months have passed since Chatham Place.
suggested_refs: Dr Thomas Gordon Hake's memoirs of Rossetti's collapse, June 1872
sources: Jan Marsh, 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti: Painter and Poet', as quoted in reachable sources

stops.name: Urrard House, Killiecrankie, Perthshire
stops.date_confidence: attested to late June 1872 for the arrival in Perthshire, with roughly nine weeks of recuperation following.
stops.campa: Hake and his son George take him north out of reach of London, and he is put up at Urrard House above the pass of Killiecrankie for nine weeks. He is convinced the walls are talking, that Browning's poems carry coded insults to him, that men on the road are agents. William Bell Scott comes to sit with him. The delusions thin out slowly through July and August. What does not thin out is the chloral, which no doctor has asked him to stop and which he now takes with whisky to make it work.
suggested_refs: Urrard House, Killiecrankie, refuge of the summer of 1872

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the second summer
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1872 for the return; day unrecorded and defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from jane_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: He returns to the manor in September to convalesce, and Jane Morris nurses him there while Morris is again in the north. He paints her as Proserpine holding the pomegranate, and as Water Willow with the manor and the river behind her head. He rises late, walks the towpath, cannot be left alone after dark. The village begins to talk. Two years of this follow. The chloral and the sleeplessness wear her down, and by 1874 she has stopped coming to him.
stops.quote: I have been here before, / But when or how I cannot tell.
stops.quote_source: 'Sudden Light', written 1854; text from Wikiquote, Dante Gabriel Rossetti
suggested_refs: 'Proserpine' (1874), Tate
'Water Willow' (1871), Delaware Art Museum

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, leaving for good
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1874 for the departure; day unrecorded and defaulted. The order of events is often reversed: the Kelmscott departure comes first, Morris's move to restructure the partnership follows in August 1874, and the formal dissolution and reconstitution as Morris and Co. falls on 31 March 1875.
stops.campa: In July he leaves the manor without ceremony and does not come back. F. S. Ellis, his publisher, takes over the co-tenancy. In August Morris moves to restructure the partnership, and the following March the firm is dissolved and reconstituted as Morris and Co. under Morris alone, with Rossetti and Ford Madox Brown paid a thousand pounds each to go and Burne-Jones and Philip Webb staying on for nothing. Rossetti keeps the money and the grievance. He is forty-six and has eight years left.
stops.quote: Look in my face; my name is Might-have-been; / I am also called No-more, Too-late, Farewell.
stops.quote_source: 'A Superscription', Sonnet XCVII of The House of Life; text from Wikiquote, Dante Gabriel Rossetti
suggested_refs: The dissolution deed of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co., 31 March 1875

stops.name: Aldwick Lodge, near Bognor Regis
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 October 1875 for the arrival, with the stay extending into 1876.
stops.campa: Theodore Watts-Dunton takes a house for him at Aldwick outside Bognor and he stays into the following year, working on Astarte Syriaca, on a new Blessed Damozel, and on portraits of his mother and of Christina Rossetti done from the two of them sitting in the same room. He walks on the shingle when he can be got out of doors. Sea air is the prescription; the chloral travels with him in the luggage. Visitors come down from London in ones and twos and compare notes with each other afterwards.
suggested_refs: 'Astarte Syriaca' (1877), Manchester Art Gallery, begun at Aldwick
Rossetti's 1877 double portrait of his mother and Christina Rossetti
sources: Rossetti Archive chronology, from the family letters

stops.name: Blake's Cottage, Felpham
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Bognor stay of 1875 to 1876; no month or day recorded, so both are defaulted. Coordinates corrected before use: the figure in circulation fell offshore in the English Channel.
stops.campa: Out along the coast at Felpham stands the flint and thatch cottage where William Blake lived three years and wrote of seeing a heaven in a wild flower, and Rossetti goes to look at it. He has known Blake since he bought the notebook as a student for ten shillings from an attendant at the British Museum, and he and his brother did as much as anyone alive to make Blake readable to the century. Blake had been dead a year when Rossetti was born. He does not record what he thought of the house.
suggested_refs: Blake's Cottage, Blakes Road, Felpham, Historic England list entry 1353792
The Rossetti Manuscript, Blake's notebook, British Library

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, Ballads and Sonnets
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 September 1881, published by Ellis and White, printed at the Chiswick Press. The claim that the volume was edited with William Michael Rossetti is false; his editorial role is posthumous, in the Collected Works of 1886 and the Works of 1911.
stops.campa: Ellis and White publish Ballads and Sonnets in September, printed at the Chiswick Press, completing The House of Life at a hundred and one sonnets and carrying Rose Mary and The King's Tragedy. He has assembled it himself with his publisher. Thomas Hall Caine, a young admirer who has moved into Cheyne Walk to keep him company and keep him upright, is in the house through the making of it and writes down what he is told. It is the last book Rossetti sees through the press.
stops.quote: Conception, my boy, FUNDAMENTAL BRAINWORK, that is what makes the difference in all art.
stops.quote_source: Rossetti to Thomas Hall Caine, in Hall Caine, 'My Story' (London: Heinemann, 1908), ch. 2.4
suggested_refs: 'Ballads and Sonnets', Ellis and White, London, 16 September 1881
sources: Rossetti Archive, Ballads and Sonnets collection introduction

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, the stroke
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 December 1881.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of December he has a stroke: the sight dims, the left side will not answer. He is fifty-three and has been taking chloral for eleven years. The doctors call it a nervous seizure and begin to speak of Bright's disease in the kidneys. Hall Caine and his mother nurse him in the house on the river he has hardly left in a decade, among the china and the mirrors and the last of the animals. He works a little at the easel with his right hand and cannot sustain it.
suggested_refs: Hall Caine's account of the winter of 1881-1882 at Cheyne Walk

stops.name: Westcliff Bungalow, Birchington-on-Sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 February 1882 for the journey down. The precise footprint of the bungalow within the town is not confirmed in sources reached; the pin is approximate to the ground between Beach Avenue and Rossetti Road.
stops.campa: The architect John P. Seddon lends him a bungalow at Birchington on the north Kent coast, on the ground between Beach Avenue and what the town later names Rossetti Road, and he is brought down in February with his mother, his sister Christina Rossetti, Hall Caine and Watts-Dunton in attendance. The prescription is the one that sent him to Bognor: sea air, quiet, distance from London. He can walk to the cliff edge on the good days. There are not many good days, and he knows the arithmetic.
suggested_refs: Rossetti Bungalow, Birchington-on-Sea, lent by the architect John P. Seddon
sources: Birchington Heritage Society archive, 'Rossetti and Birchington'

stops.name: Birchington-on-Sea, Easter Sunday
stops.date_confidence: contested to the day. The Victorian Web chronology gives 9 April 1882, Wikipedia gives 10 April and calls it Easter Sunday; Easter Sunday in 1882 fell on 9 April. Date and coordinates inherited byte-identical from jane_morris.journey.json, which carries 9 April. Not resolved.
stops.campa: He dies on Easter Sunday of Bright's disease, with his mother in the room, sixty-five days after arriving at Birchington. He is fifty-three. Jane Morris, who has been keeping her distance for years, is not there. William Michael Rossetti is, and begins that week the work of editing that will occupy him for thirty years and hand the century its collected text. Rossetti had asked in writing, six years before, to be cremated. Nobody carries the request out.
suggested_refs: William Michael Rossetti, 'The Collected Works of Dante Gabriel Rossetti', 1886

stops.name: All Saints churchyard, Birchington, the Celtic cross
stops.date_confidence: attested to mid-April 1882 for the burial; the exact day is not recorded in the sources reached and is approximate. Coordinates are the corrected church position, no atlas pin existing for the churchyard; the tomb itself lies at about 51.3735, 1.3057.
stops.campa: He is buried in the churchyard at Birchington near the south door, under a Celtic cross designed by Ford Madox Brown, who took him as a pupil thirty-four years earlier and set him to painting pickle jars. His mother, Christina Rossetti, William Michael, Watts-Dunton and Hall Caine follow the coffin. His wife lies at Highgate, a hundred miles off, in the grave he had opened. Inside the church his mother commissions two windows from Frederic Shields, one of them adapted from his own unfinished Passover in the Holy Family.
suggested_refs: Historic England list entry 1094682, 'Tomb of Dante Gabriel Rossetti in churchyard, Birchington'
The Frederic Shields memorial windows in All Saints, Birchington
